review:
This game is what i was expecting from Doom Eternal's horde mode.

Played GUNFIRE REBORN and beat the game few times with different characters but gunplay felt weak and didn't care for it so much afterwards. ROBOQUEST had better gunplay but it was way too long for what it was to finish a run and having no save system made me quit that even faster. Deadlink on the other hand ticks these two boxes flawlessly.

Faster mobility than Doom Eternal which can cause some problems at the beginning for some  people but having only 5 equipment which consist of 2 guns, 2 abilities and 1 grenade for each character/class makes it up for it in a way that you don't need to memorize so many keys and can go between these equipments fairly easily. Which will give you easier time to master the mobility.

Like Doom Eternal you can get armor from enemies you kill and you do that by marking your enemies and killing marked enemies before it expires. Grenades that damages enemies marks them for example and almost all abilities of characters also does the same thing. There are no HP recovery by killing enemies though, you only recover HP by purchasing HP from stores or by completing special rooms. Sometimes with perks. But since you can get armor from enemies way more faster and way too easily compared to Doom Eternal, you are not gonna look for HP recovery all that much, thanks to the marking system and how quick and easy you can mark enemies.

GAMEPLAY LOOP consist of you entering a room, engaging in combat in arena shooter style with very high mobility for almost all characters which can be even improved further with perks, clearing out the room and then choosing the next room. Before choosing the next room you get to see which type of rewards are you gonna get. Like how it works in HADES basically. You get perks and upgrades for your equipments after completing a room. You do this number of times and eventually enter the boss room, defeat it, and you go to the next stage where there are new enemy types in a new biome if you will. There were 3 stages in early access, now they added the 4th and final one. They also added a new character, making a total of 4 characters to choose.

All your characters have 2 weapons. One standart weapon like shotgun for soldier and one special weapon which is rocket launcher for soldier for example. Standart weapons have unlimited ammo, you just reload when magazine is empty, whereas special weapons require you to collect their ammunition in the room if there are any, or by killing enemies which they may drop it or the best and most consistent way, by breaking C-balls. C-balls are energy balls that you can find in every room and you can break them by punching them or with your certain abilities. By breaking them you do get ammo for your secondary weapon.

You have perk slots for your characters, 4 of them. Weapon switching, using ability 1, using ability 2 and breaking C-balls. 

For example soldier has a hook ability that works pretty much like super shotgun's meat hook, you fly towards that enemy and do your thing afterwards. Now if you equip a perk to your hook ability slot that says "Stun enemies that are marked (active) and deal %50 increased damage to marked enemies (passive)" it means you will stun an enemy because hook ability marks an enemy and you will deal %50 increased damage to all enemies whether you used your meat hook on them or not as long as they are marked. Active part of the perk only works when you do that action you assigned it to like using abilities or breaking C-balls. This itself creates fun and interesting builds for your character.

Soundtrack is good, it is adrenaline pumping, goes along with the gameplay itself.

I recommend this to people who craves for a good FPS roguelike because at the moment, at least for me, this is the best.

-----------------------------------------------------------

As a sidenote, the game feels at its best when you play it on higher difficulties, highest one to be exact. After getting used to playing at least 50+ runs on hardest difficulty, i chose a different character and started a run with the easiest difficulty by mistake but didn't notice it, and when the game started i thought game was bugged and not spawning enough enemies as it should. Realized later on that i was on easier difficulty. Funny side is that i was not even able to progress through first stage at the easiest difficulty when i first started playing the game but when i got used to the gameplay loop and combat, i was beating the highest difficulty with fresh save and no meta progression whatsoever. It was surely hard to achieve but it was doable. You may feel the difficulty spike at higher ones at first but once you get used to it and learn to use your mobility to your advantage, it will feel like a good and doable challenge.

Now i needed to do this because it still blews my mind how there are other roguelike FPS games that are doing better than this game, player count wise. Not that i care about the concurrent player base given that this is a single player video game but it feels like this game deserves way more attention than it got. And there are few people i saw were complaining about how difficult the game is. Because of this i wanted to talk about few more things regarding this game. Because this game is not unnecessarily hard, it is just challenging, you just have to know what type of FPS roguelike this game is. And how mobility is way more important than your combat abilities.

This is NOT Gunfire Reborn where getting few key items/weapons that you are comfortable with or having alot of meta progression makes you win the game. This game is Doom Eternal on steroids in a roguelike gameplay environment. While how this sounds may scare some people given that there were some who didn't like how Doom Eternal gameplay turned out to be, this game is actually way more managable than Doom Eternal.

In Doom Eternal you have 9 weapons. That's 9 keybinds already. There is also a button for switching between weapon's mods. That makes it 10 buttons. A grenade button and grenade switching button, which makes it 12. Chainsaw, flamethrower and punch adds up to 15 buttons. And the last one your sword or warhammer if you are playing the expansions which makes 16 buttons. And of course, dashing. 17 freaking buttons you need to go back and forth when you are dealing with your enemies which if you've played Doom Eternal on higher difficulties, you know as well as i do, you needed almost all of them.

Now if we were to check Deadlink, your characters only have 2 weapons, a grenade, 2 abilities, dash. And that's it. All of that adds up to 6 buttons you need to manage. 5, if you just use your scroll button to switch between weapons.

This is why this game is way more managable than Doom Eternal. Like in that game, you also need to switch your weapons constantly in here too but switching between just 2 weapons is alot more managable and you don't even need to press 1 or 2 by the way, you can just use your scroll button on your mouse since it is only 2 weapons. Since there aren't so many buttons you need to memorize and go back and forth, you will have easier time to learn combat controls. This will leave you to adjust how to manipulate mobility in this game because compared to Doom Eternal, this game is way more faster in a way that how your enemies come at you, how they fire at you etc. After unlocking few meta progression stuff, plus getting good at how to move, normal difficulty of the game will feel like a joke.

Just keep at it, practice your mobility, use C-balls to your advantage. If you think you are still having a hard time, go with soldier! That character has the best mobility in the game than any other character which if you master it, highest difficulty of the game will feel like walk in the park.

Overall I think the idea is solid: The upgrade system is broad with lots of options, abilities are fun to use, guns have fun gimmicks. But while I can enjoy the game for a bit, there are severe issues that hamper the experience—and the roguelite elements hold it back even more, because the amount of replay value you get from it is nonexistent. The flat colored stages with same cookiecutter enemies flooding you from all angles gets old very quickly. The focus on mobility with dashing, high jumps, and teleportation means nothing when every direction you turn there is some meatsack vying to shoot you. Decisions are split-second and you are punished harshly if you do not capitalize. Some might enjoy this, and I think I would too, but the game fails in other ways that make it more punishing and obnoxious than motivating.

When it comes to combat, which I would consider paramount to a shooter, kiting is very difficult unless you put terrain between you and the enemy that they cannot easily path around, and that is just not possible in some stage layouts. The small size of almost every arena is also very restricting, killing a lot of potential momentum. So all that is left is you, backpedaling or strafing around the same 3 or 4 types of enemy per faction, occasionally teleporting/explosion jumping if you've got the ability, every stage, every time. There is no uniqueness in that, no variety, no replayability.

Even if you're the kind to enjoy the endless slaughter of faceless mooks as I am, the enemies are the weakest part of the combat. They aren't fun to shoot and aren't fun to be shot by, and there's just not enough of them at once to hit that excessive peak where you feel like an unstoppable killing machine, which would redeem it somewhat. There's also not enough of a focus on individual battles, with every boss continually spawning the same enemies you normally fight—not even trash mobs or creeps like you'd see in other games, just all the usual enemies. And when they can dish out the usual damage too, having to contend with them [i]and[/i] the boss is just not fun. What makes the enemies worse is the their sound design, as they have very quiet movement, VO, and guns, that all tend to get lost among other sounds, which makes enemies hard to pinpoint.

Really, most every sound in the game is boring and flat, without energy and motivation; there's a lack of punchy SFX, which feels out of place for an action-packed scifi/cyberpunk shooter. All the guns, including your enemies' guns, feel like they're shooting foam darts. The music is good but also lacks fullness and presence, which in other contexts I would praise since I hate the constant ducking and overdriven clipped instruments in most modern electronic music, but when combined with the rest of the game's sound mix holds it back rather than improves it.

The thing I dislike the most about the game is a result of the above problems: It's incredibly difficult to interpret taking damage and locating enemies. It would be okay if the sound cues were better, or if the gameplay loop were more engaging, but it isn't. The "you've taken damage" screen effects last way too long; they're not instantaneous and attention-grabbing enough to make it clear you've been hit; the hit sounds lack punch and are overly busy; there is little to no visual feedback on the direction of damage taken; the quiet enemies as I described make it overly difficult to judge damage sources... I could go on. There are frequent moments where I will be getting shot from behind, or backpedal into an enemy, and not know the enemy is there, and if I'm already taking damage from somewhere, it's next to impossible to know I've begun taking more from that. In a shooter, this is very not good, and makes deaths feel unfair or unearned.

The levels could save it, but as mentioned, they are small and boring. The design is nice, but they don't do enough to stand out or make them interactable. Explosive barrels, the "C-balls" that only exist to give you ammo that you have enough of anyway, and an unlockable shell in Watts-Rucker are all you'll find while playing. There are shootable objects in the paths between arenas to unlock new items to drop, but they are placed obviously with a sound and visual effect, so there's not a feeling of accomplishment or exploration. They're just kinda there. You know to expect them after the first or second time, and after you unlock everything (which happens fast) they stop showing up. Why not have them give some credits or XP after instead?

Speaking of items, most of the upgrades are marginal and do not change your gameplay experience much. And if you really like a particular build, you just have to pray to the entropy gods that you'll get the gear you want, because the swathe of trash upgrades are going to make that difficult. One could argue that picking upgrades is a critical portion of the game, and rolling with the punches to make a build on the spot is the whole point, but forcing users to pick between multiple options that are either marginal at best or unwanted at worst, over and over again, is never good—especially when it happens so frequently (at least with me). Games like Risk of Rain do it right where almost every item is at least [i]somewhat[/i] useful or will be in the future. Yet, if you have no use for an item, the money you get for "zapping" them is pitiful, a paltry 30 or so credits, while the cheapest worthwhile mods you can buy at the shop start at 150ish. Sure, you can get 50HP back, but that's also pitiful once you start getting max health upgrades. You can't even buy it twice, so it doesn't scale.

Speaking of the player character, the devs went hard on the lore to back up your remote control robot body and to try and make the world interesting. The focus is appreciated but the delivery is not interactive, written very dry, and is lazily gamified—it feels like side content rather than a core part of the experience, which severely limits its entertainment value. Why not get codex notifications and a codex reader ingame, Metroid Prime style? Having the codex right next to the gameplay and the enemy, and making it feel like you're learning and observing as you play, adds a lot of depth and mentally links lore to enemies—it could even be tied into the upgrade system. I honestly want to read the lore and enjoy it, but it's shoved in a submenu outside of the main gameplay, so I am not given any incentive to overcome that inconvenience. The lore doesn't provide any tangible benefit to the main game either, like hints about combat styles or previously unknown weakpoints. Weakpoints are already highlighted ingame anyway, so what good does mentioning those do besides fluff?

All that can save the game are abilities and weapons at this point, and I'm pleased to say I think they're... fine. I like the versatility and unique take on the abilities, and each of the combat shells' pair of them work well together. The cooldowns are a bit high but that does tend to force you to vary your approaches. I do feel like they probably had the first two shells' gameplay designed first, and then built the rest of the game around that, because the skills and weapon mixups are clearly the meat of the game. The revolver is especially good and it always feels satisfying to land a slick headshot. All the first person animations are fluid and fun to watch, and the focus on weapon switching as a mechanic is interesting and something you don't see often.

So where from here? I don't think more enemy factions/levels will be able to salvage this game, but that's all that seems to be happening in the time I've been playing. A few gameplay tweaks here and there, but nothing to give that spark that really makes me want to pick it up and play another run. The game isn't doing anything new or interesting outside of its few one-note innovations, especially in the current trend of "boomer shooters" that play mostly just like it.

My opinion on Deadlink is divided. On one hand, I love the fast run and gun combo action that the game is going for. On the other, the game feels like it gets stale incredibly fast. By nature of the game, your run is very feast or famine, you either get what you need and thrive or don't and suffer until you inevitably get folded in half by a mob of enemies or the area's boss. As a result, I found myself regularly looking for the same implant options, shell upgrades and weapon mods. This makes the game feel like there's no real ability to have varied builds - you either have great synergies that allow you to one-shot enemies one after the other or you don't and it inevitably feels like you're bringing a peashooter to a cannon fight. There is no "Doing okay" in Deadlink, you're either doing great or terribly and praying that you find some kind of solution. If you're not dropping enemies basically instantly you're bound to be overwhelmed and cut down in practically no time.

To add to this, like many games, beating Deadlink on the default difficulty unlocks higher difficulties. I had expected the increased difficulties to provide an appreciable but fair increase in difficulty after I'd proved that I was capable of beating the default difficulty fairly consistently. But, on trying the first increase, I went from consistently beating the game to not even making it out of the first zone after attempting it for nearly two hours. The increases are fiendishly difficulty to the point that for me they're not even remotely fun. 

I'm not sure what has to be done to unlock the roughly 60% of implants I don't seem to have gotten yet, nor do I particularly care to find out. Within my roughly 10 hours of playtime the game's gotten unbelievably stale for a roguelike and there's little reason for me to consider going back to it. The game's replayability is incredibly low for the genre which in my opinion is crucial to its success or failure as a roguelike, and as a result, I cannot recommend this.

What is Deadlink? 

It's Hades... But the combat is DOOM (modern DOOM, not old-school)... With a cartoon-cyberpunk skin… And some Borderlands-style humor, let’s say Borderlands-Lite.

That's It. 

What you get: 
You get four different characters to play (unlocked as you progress), each with 2 unique weapons, and 2 unique abilities, both on cooldown timers. You have grenades, dodge, and a double-jump. 
Play through four different areas, each with an average of maybe 7 or 8ish rooms. Pick various upgrades after a room. When you die, spend some of your 2 permanent currencies to upgrade your characters and improve your drops. 
Combat has a focus on killing “marked” targets. Each character has several ways to mark a target, then when you kill said target they drop shield-refills to help you stay alive. 

You also get a timed mode, and an endless-wave hoard mode. 

The Good: 
- Combat is VERY crisp and polished
- Movement and shooting feel great
- Room rewards and meta-progression are both addictive

The Bad: 
- More repetitive than Hades, but not near as bad as some rogue-likes
- Balance of rewards is not great. Many upgrades are downright useless, while others (of the same rarity tier) are OP. (Although this does create more excitement when you get the good stuff)
- Humor falls flat most of the time
- Could not care less about the story

The Maybe:
- The highest difficulty is quite hard! (there are 3 tiers) You need to get real lucky with your upgrades, and/or spend huge amounts of currencies, which can take hours to acquire. The middle difficulty is appropriate though, far from a guaranteed completion even on a fully upgraded character.

[h2]Deadlink [/h2]

This is a decent roguelike, but more average than good. It would’ve been a “yellow” review if Steam had that option, but since it doesn’t, I’ll give it a red thumbs-down because I liked it less than I disliked it.

On the positive side, the game looks pretty good and plays quite energetically at first.

However, there are plenty of downsides: repetitive locations, a not-so-great selection of weapons and abilities, and fairly monotonous enemies.

It's a decent roguelike for those who enjoy fast-paced shooters and have already played through the best ones but still want more.

For everyone else, it’s hard to recommend. It’s just okay.

Oh man, you know that feeling when you find a game that scratches a very particular itch? When you're looking for something oddly specific and start to accept that you won't find it, but then you actually do? That's how I felt for example when I found my now go-to mecha game in M.A.S.S. Builder and this is definitely how I feel now with Deadlink. It's an absolutely stellar game and you should definitely play it.

Now what was that particular itch I'm referring to? Well I've been really into roguelikes for several years now and I've been a huge fan of anything cyberpunk for a long long time. I love everything about cyberpunk artistry. As such I played Cyberpunk 2077 and greatly enjoyed it. And the itch that I got is that I wanted a game with similar, perhaps even faster combat than 2077 but on a more casual and on-demand basis, without any of the story weight or expectation of a full RPG. A roguelike would fit perfectly in this bracket. I did find quite a few games that tackle this, kind of, but it was always not exactly what I was imagining. Roboquest, Mothergunship, CyberCorp, Synthetik, GTTOD, I See Red. All of those are amazing games and I recommend them too, but they weren't able to nail the vibe I was looking for. Enter Deadlink, a game that is EXACTLY what I'm looking for.

A cyberpunk roguelike first-person shooter with fast-paced gameplay, great mobility, great aesthetics and a banging soundtrack. All the boxes are checked! Now, this game does tend to fall almost too neatly into the stereotypes and cliches of the genre, but honestly, that's completely fine. If you choose a well known aesthetic like this, there is nothing wrong with doubling down and giving people exactly what they expect. The game knows exactly what people are going to expect and is more than happy to deliver. Towering skyscrapers, dirty streets, an overcrowded, massive, neon-drenched metropolis, complete with sex stores and vending machines on every corner, gratuitous advertising and cameras on every wall, pastiches of Japanese culture, cyborg soldiers, gangsters and street thugs, drones, evil laboratories, endless warehouses, references to 3D printing, cryptocurrencies and AI as everyday things, and more. All of the classic elements of cyberpunk culture are present in the visuals and the story. Speaking of which the story itself is quite stereotypical, but quite engaging too. You upload your consciousness into a bio-mechanical body, roam the streets of the massive gigacity, fighting back against cyborg yakuza, ninja geisha robots, cyber sumo wrestlers and robot tanks . Then you can storm the halls of a German biotechnology lab or the warehouses of communist Giga Amazon (yes, really) and face the countless techno-organic monstrosities hidden within. The story tells a classic but still engaging tale of government conspiracy, corporate hegemony, transhumanism and misery in a futuristic world. The soundtrack is also exactly what you need to fit all this and it's an absolute banger. I could go on and on but to put it briefly, if you love the cyberpunk genre, this game is a must play. You will absolutely love it.

And my personal story and bias aside, Deadlink is a genuinely awesome game. It's gameplay-wise really similar to Doom Eternal actually, even the armour pickup sound is almost the same. It has great visuals that are stylized and realistic at the same time, the movement and gunplay are both super tight and responsive, there's a decent variety of abilities and weapons and a very unique and varied upgrade system. The roguelike elements as always keep the experience engaging and interesting. The only criticism I can give is that the game is a bit slim on content at the moment, but this is understandable as it's still in early access. The devs have already released quite some stuff post launch, so I know they are dedicated to improving this. There is more than enough content as is and the game is still tons of fun. Come on and go kill some corpo scum!

The core gameplay is fun and satisfying, but it is a good example of a roguelite which just pads playtime through repetition.
When you play this game, you will play with your choice of 4 classes through the same four levels with the same bosses again and again. You will grind out your upgrade currencies to get further, but your runs will very soon all feel the same. Levels aren't varied enough and mods feel too passive to make different runs stand out from each other.

This is a shame, if this game managed to make each run feel more unique with interesting strategies to take, it would hold out much longer. But as it stands, it doesn't matter if your gun shoots blue or red balls, a run with each class will always feel the same.

Get it on sale and if you're not put off by repetition. Otherwise look for the plethora of other Boomer Shooters.

This game wakes me up better than coffee in the morning. 

The combination of roguelite and action shooter elements makes for a really addictive and challenging gameplay loop. Likely just me, but when I have a god tier build and my first thought is "Can't wait to see how I screw this one up," I know the game is challenging. You can have absolute perfection crumble due to poor execution, which may suck, but at the same time, you also have the opportunity to have dogshit make it through to the final boss due to perfect execution. That's only somewhat true come Neuromancy difficulty, but it's so minimal that it's really only worth mentioning as a sidenote for disclaimer's sake. 

I would say for 95% of the time, the success of a run comes down to player skill with the randomized elements adding nice little touches/challenges to give you a boost along the way. The levels are limited (4 currently) but the challenges offered the higher you climb in difficulty combined with the soundtrack and variability afforded via randomized upgrades/enemy comps keeps you sufficiently engaged for an arguably bite-sized package. At the highest difficulty (Neuromancy) each run can take anywhere from 30 minutes (we'll get into that) to an hour to complete based on loadout.

For those of you that are super into story, there's not a whole lot here. There's some gradual developments that are made following each run a la Hades, but don't expect it to be as in-depth as that game (which I'm not saying it should be considering this is Gruby's first game vs. Supergiant's 4th(?)). Still entertaining though. The more subtle world-building elements are rather creative and lively, and the game actually has a good sense of humor. Never thought I would play an action-cyberpunk-roguelite where one of the enemies is just there to take the piss out of Elizabeth Holmes.  

That's my high-level review, anyways. I got some more itemized elements to lay out, though, starting with the good (note a lot of these pertain to Neuromancy difficulty as that's basically the endgame):
-Soundtrack, as I said, really tight. Feels like it's in rhythm with the combat in a lot of cases.
-Enemies are exceptionally varied in terms of attack patterns and threat priority which keeps combat very dynamic as more enemies spawn in.
-No wasted space for combat. You are using everything at your disposal and it rarely ever feels clunky, even at the lower levels where you may have less tools in your arsenal.
-Each reward path has its own intrinsic merit where the value of each is able to shift depending upon the state of your run so you rarely have a "Yeah sure fine if there's nothing else," moment.

That being said, here are the criticisms:
-That 5% where your runs are in the hands of the game? It's Toxic damage. Enemies in Neuromancy all have armor so it's kind of mandatory. The only upside: it's not that had to get on either your light or heavy weapon.
-Hunter shell feels off? Lower health, less opportunities to mark, relies on getting the drop on enemies. Should be a highly mobile glass cannon right? Not really. Even with extreme precision, time to kill is either on par or lower than other frames with comparative buffs, its CDs are high, and it doesn't fix the issue where options to mark enemies are limited, which, if you aren't killing marks, you're dying FAST. (Sidenote: I could also really suck at this character.)
-The Hammer Bros before the last boss feel supremely overtuned. Unless I am playing the Juggernaut shell, I fear for my life every time I step into that encounter. They can be beaten, yes, but they single-handedly have ended more of my runs than anything else in the game. (Again I could also just suck at these guys.)
-Phoenix shielders are legitimately no fun. Fast gunplay screeches to a halt when these losers instant transmission into your pristine headshot and proceed to sit there waiting to poke their head out so you can shoot them, before they duck back behind the shield again. At least the sumos incentivize you outmaneuvering them.
-Thoughts are torn on Iskra. I find it interesting that the two most challenging parts of the fight last the longest on Neuromancy and even lead to an overlapping of mechanics. I know I don't like the fact that hitting the weakpoints on the first and third phases basically require you to be in direct line of fire. Otherwise, pretty solid chaos fight.

This is a bit rambly, so TL;DR the game is ok, but the second half of each run is more frustrating than fun, the player's damage feels too low most of the time (seriously, even on a good run, the final boss took 10 real life human minutes to beat in a game as fast as this. Plus another 5 for phase 2), and the meta-progression (permanent upgrades bought outside runs) feels unnecessary. If you want an arena fps roguelite/roguelike, BPM: Bullets Per Minute is a ton of fun. If you just want an arena fps... play Doom, Quake, Boltgun, or Ultrakill (especially Ultrakill). I'd rather buy any of those games at full price than buy this game sale, but if you really want to give this a go, wait for at least a 50% off sale. Finally, I apologize if the following is more of a rant than a review. I had more pent up frustration toward this game than I thought, but I stand by my issues with the game, even without the salt. This review would've been positive before the 1.0 changes, but they just had to fix what wasn't broken and fucked up the enemy armor system and in run progression, ruining the most important part of a game, especially an arena shooter, the gameplay.

It's fine for a bit, then you realize there are 2 kinds of runs in this game.

1. You basically one shot everything and have little to no issues the entire run
2. You tickle fodder enemies, let alone heavy enemies and bosses. If you win runs like this, it's a slog consisting of 20 minute boss fights and running away from enemies because you don't have enough damage to kill them before they kill you.

Floors 1 and 2 are good, 1 being the best imo. Floors 3 and 4 are just not fun at all. Honestly, I'd be fine if they went back to runs ending after the second boss just so I don't have to deal with the second half of the game. The C-Ball grabbing enemies on floor 3 are a good idea in concept because it shares a resource with you, forcing you to kill them so you can keep your constant supply of heavy ammo. But they only take one ball at a time, so that part is a non issue, but if they get a single C-Ball, they get full armor immediately then start running away, forcing you to chase them because their C-Ball can only be broken by melee. Soldier and now Juggernaut can deal with them pretty well, Soldier because he can just grapple to them so they can't get away, Juggernaut because his F ability breaks the C-Ball they're carrying and his Q let's him close the distance. Hunter has a hard time with them because his mobility is a swap, so you rely on an enemy being near them to catch up. Engineer can't kill much of anything, so of course he has a hard time, too. It's not like you can just ignore them, either, especially the healer. The non healer does a ton of damage, so you have to chase to get rid of the threat, and the healing ones heal other enemies, forcing you to prioritize them. The boss is also not good. The arena feels like it was designed for a different game. Soldier feels like he's the only one with enough mobility to maybe have fun in the fight because of how vertical the arena gets throughout the fight, but regardless of who you're playing, you have to listen to the same 4 voice lines from the boss on repeat while fighting it, which is the worst part of the boss. The 4th floor is just a series of mini boss encounters with recycled enemies from previous floors leading up to a final boss that is by far the worst part of the game. She's fast and hard to hit, has pretty hard to dodge attacks, and has the health bar of a Destiny strike boss. She's a bullet sponge in the worst way possible. She cycles through the same few attacks while you scramble around the arena for an enemy to kill for shields and deal so little damage to her you can't even see her health bar move. And after spending 10 minutes killing her, she has another phase that's the exact same as the first one, only she's faster, makes clones while going invisible, and her attacks are purple instead of red. You can lower her max HP by doing all the rooms leading up to her fight, but even then she still takes way too long to kill. It's not a challenge, it's an endurance test, and this game is not designed for an endurance test.

The combat shells (characters) are hit and miss. Soldier has a grappling hook and a shotgun, giving him a very clear high mobility, high damage playstyle. Juggernaut plays similarly, but has a dash and damage negation instead of the grapple. These are my favorite shells, with Hunter coming in close behind. Hunter's stealth is a very good tool and his revolver doesn't do bad damage. Then there's Engineer. I've never seen a more useless character in any game. His guns do no damage, his Q is both his only CC and his only mobility (not to mention the aoe damage on killing the target), and his turret also doesn't do any damage, but you have to use it because it does more than your weapons do together. The intent of the character is clearly to have a more space control focused playstyle, but the damage numbers make no sense. Other shells can salvage a bad run, this character basically requires a god run just to function.

Builds are also much more restrictive than it originally seems. The implant system is a great idea and I love how modular it is. However, the only viable build seems to be toxic damage. Toxic has the best implants that I can find and as far as I can tell not a single enemy is resistant to it, unlike other damage types. After release, it seems that they want all your power to come from the implants. But up until release, you got way more neuralboost upgrades, which boost stats like max hp, damage, skill power etc. This meant that even if you didn't get a great run, you still did damage through sheer force of big numbers. Now, you get far fewer of those upgrades, which means your build rests heavily on the implants you get, but since few of them give stat bonuses, even with good abilities from implants you don't do much damage. This is another reason toxic seems to be the only viable option now because some implants let you apply corrosion, which deals toxic damage over time. Another implant spreads corrosion to nearby enemies with an enemy dies with corrosion on them. Toxic ends up being the best damage type without damage upgrades because it deals damage so often, and toxic is still the best damage type with damage upgrades for the same reason. 

Finally, the armor system. Before release, enemy armor was basically a shield over their hp you had to get through before touching their actual health bar. Toxic was made to strip this armor, so of course it was also incredibly powerful with this version of armor, too. Now, armor is damage reduction instead. This change makes no sense to me because as it is now, the armor just makes your already low damage feel even lower since your damage is split between the enemy's hp bar and the tiny little strip at the bottom of their hp bar that represents their armor. The old system put all your damage to the armor, then all your damage to the hp once you were through, which meant that even without toxic to quickly deal with armor you still felt like you hit like a bus because you could see all the damage reflected on the enemy's hp very easily. The new armor system also raised the time to kill, to the point that fodder enemies can tank multiple shots from a heavy weapon (i.e. more than 2 shots max), or in the case of beam weapons, it can take multiple full seconds of just holding left click on a fodder enemy before they die. 

The gameplay can be fixed basically by just reverting the changes from the 1.0 patch. The 3rd floor boss would probably be much more tolerable if the platforms didn't raise up so high and if the voice lines were just removed (seriously, the voice lines are the worst part of the fight. It's so grating). The final boss just needs less hp and a smaller arena so you don't have to walk across a country to get to an enemy for shields mid fight.

Gonna be honest, not sure why this is so highly rated, I had to double take to make sure this was full release and not still EA. Figure it's just people playing 2-3 hours(when it's fresh and fun) then just not going back to the game/revising their review later on, because this game has some of the worst replayability and balance.

Biggest gripes are the balance and lack of variety(in just about everything). First difficulty level felt like a good intro, nothing felt unfair, bosses weren't complete ass to deal with with mediocre loadouts. Second level you start seeing that some weapons are just completely unusable and you wonder if you're missing something - nope, just bad design. Bosses(the same 4, the only 4, the only 4) start to get a bit stale and gimmicky. Third difficulty is just fishing for an Arc Cannon on loadout select or restarting, because literally everything else is many leagues below it. Bosses and enemies in general getting the 40%(+?) movement speed starts to show just how badly the movement and collision is in the game. Everything takes 3x to kill because of the dogtier armor/shield system the game has. Still all of the same encounters, just mega aids now. The final boss glitches out and gets stuck in place every fight, but it's fine because the fight itself is so trash you're just happy to finish the run. It's like playing melee in a fight where the ai has infinite teleports and no cooldown on them.

The way the passive/actives(not class abilities but the nodes or whatever they're called) is actually a neat system, most of the node themselves are super lackluster but some actually change the way you play and at least early on you have to make choices on your limited slots, something that goes away once you start unlocking the progression tree. Speaking of the tree, the economy in this game is so stingy, it's made in a way that it'd take 15+ hours to likely unlock everything, which would actually be on the lower end for a roguelike, thing is this game doesn't have the content to back that up so artificially dragging it is just frustrating. The fact you don't get more experience/currency on stage 4 compared to stage 1 is also bad design, it'd be more efficient to spam the first level on Diff. 3 then do the all 4 stages because the reward per room/boss is the exact same from your first encounter to your final.

A lot of the enemies just feel awful to fight against - shield bros(both the Sumo guys and Mr Tower shields) are complete ass design. The exosuit enemies that grab orbs and mega buff/heal/turn on turrets are atrocious in their hitbox and lack of ranged options. The way bigger enemies on the highest difficulty can literally body block you while they have the Flash's speed and just gangbang you.. list goes on. Harder shouldn't equate making bullet sponges or just increasing a slider on the mobs stats. Make more environmental hazards, new mechanics, risk v reward objectives. This game fails in its design of difficulty by turning numbers up for the AI, and down for the player, it's not fun. 

Outside of the stale encounter design, I was disappointed in how little content the game seemed to offer as a roguelike as well. The stages aren't varied, it's the same tilesets which are all reused, there is zero pro-gen involved and the pool per map is very low, you'll see every tileset within 2-3 visits to the locale and it gets old very quickly. Each class has a single primary, with the primaries and their upgrades in general being fairly lackluster and you'd have to get an insane gambit to even have them be your "primary" through the run. The secondary(what actually does damage) options do actually have some variety, but you'll soon find out the only things worth using are explosives and the arc cannon, with everything else getting severely outclassed. You also can just get the best weapons/upgrades upon starting the run.. so most people will just do that. There is just so little thought put into some of these systems when there are so so so many good roguelikes out there that showcase exactly why this sort of design is trash.

The music and art design are both super good and immersive, there just isn't much variety in either. The first few hours/runs as you're unlocking new stuff and things are still fresh are great, but once that honeymoon phase is over you see just how shallow the game is. 10 hours to clear on the hardest difficulty with 2 classes, probably only 5-6 hours of enjoyment from it. For $20 there are worse offenders, but honestly if you're reading reviews to see if you want to try this you care about the cost, and there are many, many better options to spend it on.

I really want to like this game, I can see where the base formula would work to be an amazing, fast-paced shooter. My issues are twofold: inconsistent pacing and grinding for content.

There is a lot you need to manage in any firefight, button mashing and holding left click is a recipe for certain failure. The cognitive burden is not too high, there are systems that make it more appealing to mix and match your weapons and tools to be your most effective. The problem comes in when you don't reach a flow early, miss your timings, or fall out of your flow for a moment. The enemies are close, the weapons are slow to reload, and your tools have a timer, so that minor break causes the action to screech to a halt while you slap on another mag like your life doesn't depend on it.

The game is a roguelite, so there is a persistent upgrade tree in that sense; however, where other roguelites offer some flexibility to change or adapt builds within or between runs, you enter a run with a set class and are allowed modifiers on what that class brings to the table. No weapon changes and not many movement differences. There are currently only three classes available, one of which is locked behind a certain amount of progress through the areas, thus either of the remaining two are your only options when starting out. I just want to shoot things in a variety of ways and on an increasing power scale, but Deadlink feels like it's holding back for reasons I don't claim to understand.

I got the impression that the developers are worried about giving their players too much agency or power, that the fun should be derived from the repetitive and practiced aspects of the gameplay and the sense of progression is a secondary consideration. The feeling I get from a strong run in Roboquest or Hades or Risk of Rain 2 just isn't in this package at the moment.

Deadlink is a two-hour game that desperately tries to convince you that it has more to deliver.

The basic loop is satisfying enough: go into dungeon, shoot mans, dodge their shooting back, tag them with certain abilities that make them loot pinata like in Doom 2016. In fact, the basic loop is very Doom 2016 encouraging you to push forward and explode things so they give you armor and ammo.

The problem is that it has a completely unwanted and un-necessary roguelite thing grafted to it where when you die, you go back to start, you pay for a few upgrades with metacurrency, you dive back in again. This is not, fundamentally, a bad idea. I've loved plenty of Roguelites and I enjoy the idea of unlocking more options and coming back again to see what exciting new twists the RNG has thrown on to the table.

The problem is that there is a very small amount of arenas, you will see all of them on one run, and the game has no more up its sleeve. The same goes for the enemies, no randomness, you will see the entire pack. Bosses? Yep, one per biome, seen them once, seen them all. What about the loadout, though? Are there surprises there? Yes, and they're all bad. There's exactly one good secondary weapon and if you don't get that, my experience is that you may as well ignore the slot(the basic rocket launcher with the no-self-harm upgrade is what I'm referring to, being able to grapple over to enemies and explode right on top of them is genuinely a bit OP).

But what about the classes, or "shells" as Deadlink calls them? Well, a lot of games with this formula start you off with a bad class and it's a relief when you get better ones that can break the game more but... Deadlink just starts you off with the best one. The others may have other mechanics or be more sturdy but... the basic one has the best starting weapons, a balanced durability and the game's best mobility option. No reason to play anything else.

So, in one run, you have seen everything. What's the point of more runs, then when you beat that? Higher difficulties. Ah, yes, with new arenas? New mutators? New enemies and challenges? Aside from one really annoying one where you have to punch ammo boxes a lot and a wave survival gimmick event, I didn't see any that did anything other than make the enemies spongier. Which really took away a lot of the fun, it slowed down the game a lot. It should've just dropped more enemies or made them hit harder, maybe given you less options for healing. But making enemies more durable, I feel, was a mistake. It makes your guns feel wimpy and sabotages one of the core joys which was a low time-to-kill for all non-boss enemies.

The fourth biome also has a couple of minibosses with mechanics that the game does not deign to explain(the only self-healing and genuinely invincible enemies in the game, any sort of explainer or lower-level enemy using the same sort of behavior would've been a good help in making them not feel kind of puzzling to fight the first time around).

So anyway, Deadlink flubbed its core concept on almost every level. If you want the same sort of high mobility, high risk gameplay but shorn of all the pointless parts, I would recommend just playing Ultrakill.

The one caveat to this review is that I got bored halfway through the middle difficulty and its possible that the highest difficulty would've totally wowed me, but I feel like there's roughly an 0.0001% chance of that.

The combat is fluid, fast and rewards constantly marking enemies to ensure you survive the combat long enough. With ample means to upgrade and enhance yourself to be a fine-tuned killing machine while listening to a fantastic music track that does not distract from the gameplay and the enjoyment...keeping you immersed.

...And this is where the good points kind of falls off a cliff.
While the combat is fluid and can be challenging, certain aspects prove to be overwhelming or tedious.
Examples are as follows:

1. The second boss, upon entering the second phase, is less capable of being hit. Not a big deal, enemies keep spawning in to keep your shields up. Good. But then there is that ship that spews out homing fast-moving mines that, while you can shoot them and the ship to destroy it, chances are the moment you killed it and turn your attention to the boss...within 3 seconds another of that ship has spawned in and is making more mines and you still can't hit the boss. It's not a hard fight but it is horrendously [b]tedious[/b] and drags out the fight with artificial difficulty where because you have dedicated a lot of time to fight this thing it gives the illusion of being hard rather than seen for what it actually is: micromanaging.

2. The third boss is a good challenge, but the only part of it that is brutal is the very first phase where most of the floor ends up electrified and then the boss itself shoots out a wide-arc attack. If it wasn't for me playing Soldier a lot and having a grapple to pull myself up off the ground away from it all using the flying robots...I can't help but wonder how well the other combat shells would do. But also there are times the momentum of the grapple will launch me out so far that I land in electrified terrain and end up dying anyway. This wasn't a huge deal, but then the rest of the fight is just maintaining shields and shooting until it dies. The difficulty curve turns into a cliffside and nosedives after the first phase which is the literal only hurdle in that fight.

3. This was the point that was the last straw that broke the camel's back, as one would say. In the fourth zone, every room you go to has a miniboss challenge. Not a big deal at face value, except when one of those minibosses is a teleporting enemy who pops up, attacks, then shortly teleports again. Not a big deal, just stun and shoot...right? Sure. But then there's lots of enemies rushing you, sniping enemies stuck to the walls that keep coming in even after you kill them. And if you take time to try regain shields, you better hope the miniboss hasn't teleported away and is nowhere to be seen. This happened several times, and when she is just gone...she shows up after she has regenerated from being half-dead to about 90% healthy with rapidly regenerating health.
After doing this endless battle with me replenishing shields but unable to kill her despite every shot I do being over 500 damage or so to the face with every element on that shotgun, doing more damage on the first shot when I grapple in on her...I quite literally just got frustrated at the stupidity of the entire fight and closed out of the game with no intention of ever picking the game back up in its present state.

Play this game if you want to just chill and mindlessly kill things, but don't expect to get far anytime soon without countless hours of grinding and dumb luck.

Deadlink is a decent but flawed rogue-like FPS. The game has an impressive soundtrack, art style, and the performance is really good. I enjoyed playing the fast-paced gameplay for the first couple of hours.

Unfortunately, after the first completed run there's not much else different to experience, and as a rogue-like that's not a good thing. Replayability suffers due to the lack of variety of enemies, arenas, and impactful implants. The rogue-like build options like the elemental upgrades have hardly any effect on how the game plays. There are implants to choose from during runs, but they're small upgrades that don't drastically change the way you play throughout. Meta upgrades can be purchased outside of the simulation. I also didn't really care for the additional armor that enemies have at higher difficulty as this just made the combat feel more tedious.

Ultimately, I think Deadlink is worth playing, but not for very long as the combat loop wasn't designed well enough to keep me playing over and over again. 

Purchase on sale if you're interested.

If you like how Doom Eternal (or Quake, or other similar boomer shooters) feel in terms of combat and movement then you'll probably enjoy this.

There are four classes which all play pretty differently from one another, along with a ton of different upgrades to find and try out. I was pretty skeptical at the concept of a roguelike FPS at first but you can make some genuinely wacky and fun loadouts by combining these various upgrades, such as having the Soldier's grappling hook ability ignite and poison its target, along with instantly recharging if you happen to kill them before you finish zipping to them.

The variety and wackiness helps keep the game pretty fresh despite there only being four stages (with each stage having like 8 encounters + a boss) per run, which will probably run you 30 minutes or so depending on how things go.

There's also an overarching story to uncover although it's mostly just watching a different cutscene each time you manage to beat the final boss and finish a run. I think it could stand to be slightly cheaper but I don't regret buying it and it's a lot of fun when you just want to jump in for an hour or so and shoot stuff.

There are three difficulty settings and in general you can make almost any class + loadout work on the first two difficulties if you are skilled enough. Difficulty 2 feels like the 'sweet spot' once you get used to it, as it will remain decently challenging even after you buy upgrades.

For the highest difficulty however, you are at the complete mercy of the RNG to get enough DPS/regen to stand a chance. In a way this makes sense since it's not supposed to be fair, but I think the enemies could still do with an armor reduction as the extra speed and harder spawn patterns more than make the experience excruciating. Going into a roguelike and *especially* a shooter with low-to-middling DPS is never fun when you have giant stacks of armor on even the basic enemies. It just doesn't feel good.

Aside from this and some minor polish issues (some of the animations look a little stiff, there are a few typos here and there, and the portraits for characters keep on talking even after their lines have been read) this game is solid overall and worth your time if you enjoy frantic arena-shooter action along with some roguelike mechanics to spice things up.

The best worst game I've played in a while. 

I was mega hyped for it, love Roguelites and Doom and through something that's both of those should be amazing. Sadly, the game is great but frustratingly shit, for a few clear reasons. Gun play feels and looks good, loot is generally satisfying, and the game looks and sounds great. 

1) Core mechanic creates its own bag of problems. The game *requires* you to mark and kill marked enemies to regenerate shield and ammo. At high difficulties, mark time is very low, and only your abilities and grenades can mark things. Cooldowns on your abilities are all absurdly long (unless you're lucky with a cooldown implant or cheesing with a reset item/implant/shell upgrade). This leads not to incredibly engaged gameplay where you're weaving in and out from enemies, soaking up damage but taking them on to regenerate at risk, but instead blowing all your cooldowns, gathering a bit of shield, and then running away to ledges and temp sheilf pick-ups until your abilities are back. Entirely antifun. Especially terrible at higher levels when enemies tank rockets to the face like they're popcorn balls and marks last a second or two. 

2) Difficult spike is a flat wall that drops off if you've been godtier lucky enough to get your "build" online. The cooldown/mark/run around loop means that in high difficulties where dozens of enemies spawn all at once, your ass is toast. Once in a blue moon, however, you'll get a cheese combo of shell upgrades, implants, etc that make the game AFK easy. Then you go back to dying for 100 runs in a row. I finished the last boss on the hardest difficulty without even realising it, because my engineer turret had ability power, fire+elec+toxic, and burst down the boss in, I kid you not, literal seconds. 

3) The game is far too RNG reliant. See above. You'll go literally hundreds of runs not seeing a certain implant because you only have three rerolls (oh and your rerolls are shared between any choice, so you'll get a shit weapon but can't reroll cos you want to spend it on rerolling an implant). 

4) Enemies either swarm the shit out of you . It goes beyond Chaotic to simply stupid, especially when their tankiness comes up in higher difficulties. Then three mortar tanks spawn, plus three charger shield guys, plus two teleport witches, basically there's no where to go (oh don't stop moving because the tanks will obliterate you, but also don't run out of dashes or jumps because the witch will get you, but also don't even think about touching the ground because the chargers take no damage and are faster than you). Oh, "just hit them from behind!" lmao, sure, just jump over them and stand there while witches and tanks take their turns with your exposed cheeks. 

5) you're so slow. Sure, you can move faster, but then all your implants and shell upgrades are no longer giving you damage. So you can choose to be fast and do zero dps, or slow and enemies take three rockets to kill. lol.

6) certain Characters/frames/robots are just not really viable. At higher difficulties the hunter is fun but not viable. You need to mark enemies to survive, remember? But your swap ability MUST be reserved for traversal (nice cooldown penalty if you use it on an enemy, oh and it swaps you INTO the enemies on the ground). You can go invisible every 16 seconds or whatever, hope you enjoy your one attack you get that does double damage (so you still need to shoot the enemy once more to kill it). 

7) meta progression is the slowest thing on earth. After nearly 30 hours I still don't have all the upgrade paths unlocked. Some of the late upgrades seem core parts of the characters kit, why would they be locked away behind 5000 fucking credits? 

8) nerfs. Why would you nerf anything in a PVE single-player game? Especially when disgusting cheese strats and builds still exists, it's not just gated behind some of the most unforgiving RNG in roguelite history. 

All in all, a fantastic game that's been put together with real love, but severe flaws in the design that end up making it a pure slog. I'd highly recommend it if you're looking for something to enjoy and a few dozen hours before realising you actually are having no fun, really, and dropping it entirely. You'll definitely get caught by the "this is fun, and I'm sure with just one more upgrade and some good RNG I'll get the C-ball invisibility implant or the one that restores 40% of my cooldown. Just one more run".

I'm not normally a big roguelike fan, but this one hooked me.  It's a well-tuned combination of the roguelike mechanic (with a skill tree that grants permanent upgrades) and FPS gameplay.  

Pros:  

- The game slowly adds mechanics as you play, so despite the depth of what there is to do here, it is never overwhelming.  
- Progression feels natural and steady.  It's usually not difficult to add a new skill from the skill tree every few runs, which keeps the game feeling fresh.  
- 4 different character classes also helps with replayability.  At 15 hours of gameplay, I've really only focused on 1 of those classes, and have hardly touched the other 3.
- The FPS combat itself is well-crafted.  Movement feels fluid, and the combat is satisfying.  The inclusion of "stages" is also a nice touch- the transition from one stage to the next gives you a minute to relax and prepare yourself mentally for the next round of combat.  

Cons:

- There's some variation/randomness to the stages that you work your way through, but honestly a bit more variety in this would be nice.  It doesn't take long before the level architecture starts to get kind of stale.  
- The soundtrack isn't bad, but it's also just kind of... there. I think the game would really benefit from a dynamic soundtrack that changes in response to your actions and the environment in the moment.
Bosses are too large to swap places with and they can see you when you're invisible.  I'm sure glad I chose the class whose only two abilities are swapping places with enemies and turning invisible.

Not only that the powerups in this game sadly feel terrible and the shield regeneration mechanic is poorly thought out. Most of the powerups are your typical increase damage by 10%, increase shields by 10%, increase health by 10% and while those kind of upgrades are certainly necessary in rougelike/lite games, almost every upgrade in this game is some kind of variant of that. As for the shields, you have to mark enemies by using your abilities almost constantly. This makes it feel like you are required to use your abilities all the time in order to keep your health up, rather then being able to make more strategic choices for when to use them. Overall, the game feels like a solid fps shooter with rougelike elements added at the last moment.

So far this has been an incredibly enjoyable Rogue-lite FPS with combat that reminds me of doom 2016 in both it's high emphasis on mobility and resource management involving incredibly aggressive play. The cyberpunk aesthetic and cell-shaded art-style mixing both strong pastels and vibrant neon's really appeals to me and I've enjoyed challenging myself with the higher difficulties. My main complaints are mostly to do with it's limited content offerings. The game currently only has two classes (although I truly love how different their kits are) and two locations (with many arenas between them, but they are becoming repetitive at 10 hours of play, especially the Japanese levels. However as this is so close to the early access release, I fully expect this to become rectified as development progresses. One problem more content will not necessarily fix is the game's unfortunate, in my opinion, over-reliance on persistent upgrades as progression. Obviously these are a source of contention for discussions of the Rogue like and lite subgenres, and I have personally really enjoyed games with persistent stat increases to their game loops like Hades and Gunfire Reborn. However persistent upgrades in Deadlink go from the convenient like expanded pick up radius, new abilities, and getting a loadout after spawning just to mix up each run more fully and experiment early, to the compulsory persistent damage, resistance, and health sometimes totaling at buffs of nearly 25%. This feels like it is compensating for the game's speed (projectiles, player, and enemy) instead of making other ways the player can keep up with enemy health and dps. Altogether I really have enjoyed this title and look forward to future updates and content.

Imagine DOOM (2016) and Cyberpunk had a baby, and it turned out as a roguelite. Deadlink is, simply put, a challenging adrenaline-filled masterpiece that will keep you on your toes from start to finish.

...It's ok, I guess. 
Deadlink, at it's core, is a unique take on the roguelike genre. Instead of upgrades being passive or activating on hit/kill, your upgrades activate after swapping weapons, using abilities, or smashing a 'c-ball' which are ammo crates. 
The upgrades also have a battery meter, which means that the ability's active ability cannot be used unless you equip it on an ability that does not have the correct battery meter. This is a pretty unique balancing system that I like a lot. It stops you from getting too strong too fast, but the issue is that you never really feel like you're getting stronger. 
Not only is there a lack of that feeling, every run plays systematical the same. There's hasn't been a run where I've gotten an upgrade and it's changed the entire way I play the game. With other games in the genre like Gunfire that DOES have upgrades that dramatically change a run, it feels bad to do the same thing for 25 minutes straight.
Deadlink is also far more skill-based than other roguelikes, which is enjoyable until you realize you have no clue where you're being hit from or where the enemies are. Half the time you don't even realize you're taking damage then BOOM you're dead. There is no healing in this game other than medkits you get after completing a room. Your survivability is based entirely on 'marking' enemies with your abilities and grenades then killing them for shield. This is done well but you get a minuscule amount of shields from enemies that can be way too sponge-y.
Deadlink has so much potential but not only does this not feel like a full release, there is nothing here that isn't done better by other games. Roboquest has waaay better feeling gunplay and Gunfire Reborn has waaay better roguelike elements. I want to like this game, but when you have bullshit deaths from who knows where and when runs feel stale and boring after the first area, you're doing something wrong.

But you activate it like that, and thereafter if you kill them during their short 'Marked' state, they'll replenish your ammo for both your shotgun & rocket launcher by 1 ammo count, respectively. And you don't have to reload them, they're just instantly there. That's [b] INSANE [/b]! I love it, I adore it, I squeal & piss over it. That's downright beautiful -- what a wonderful system.
Such means that if you're playing good; by 'Marking' enemies commonly & weapon-switching, you won't ever even need to reload, nor keep track of your ammo counts. Wow. That's a really cool enforcer!

The maps are really well-made as well. I feel the 1st level's map are maybe a little too flat in retrospective. But The 2nd level's map are straight-up fantastic! I love how many unique ideas there's been thrown in there, with ideologies within the maps which I've never seen replicated truly akin in any other games. I adore how many platforms there typically are, and how many unique layers & heights there are to them. Many parts of the 2nd level's maps are so beautifully constructed as to push truly special game-play scenarios, with its more airborne drone enemies as well. All very cool!

The guns feel great as well, they have a lot of punch & kick in them. I love how devastating the rocket launcher is... for my corpses that is. That's just crazy!... ass... frog...
They all look & feel great in every way.
How the guns represent their unique weapon mods you've chosen to adapt to them are very cool; as that both looks cool & is very useful as a reminder.
Albeit I feel like sometimes my shotgun blasts -- specifically & exclusively -- just goes through enemies sometimes. I'm not sure if it's a glitch or what's up. Maybe I just need to call my dad & admit that I'm a no good gamer? Who knows?
It's just not something I feel I experience in many other games.

But over-all, such a banger.



[h1] Rogue-lite [/h1]

As said previously above, I'm like rogue-lite hater #1. I've never been a fan of the formula, and I feel like like it's a lazy & safe formula typically adapted only to tack as much play-time unto games -- as to raise the play-time; with less work than making an actual 8-10 hour static campaign. You're welcome to argue with me in the comments. Cya!

But here... here I don't mind too much.
Compared to something like Hades; in its current state Deadlink is 1000% more enjoyable for me. That's mostly due to how it's not as grindy; as I've already unlocked most of the upgrades for my character within my first 4 hours, from maybe only ~8 runs. And as of now -- in 'Early Access' -- the campaign is very short, and very straightforward. I can appreciate that. There's only 2 levels to beat, and runs seem much faster & less RNG-focused. Cool!
So once you die (and you [b] WILL [/b] die), it really won't be the same amount of hassle, at least not for me. And a majour part of that is also due to how great the combat itself is, it's not just 'good', it's not just 'great. It's 'fantastic'!
It's so darn brilliant, that I feel inclined to mostly overlook it, because what I love about the game heftily overshadows the parts I do not.



[h1] Cyberpunk, Cyberfunk [/h1]

The world of Deadlink is beautiful & immensely gorgeous. There are a ton of scenic vistas, which feel almost like screenshot-bait to focus on in-between fights... and I accept it... because I adapt it. lol
It's so freaking awesome & amazing! Both of the levels so far are wonderfully constructed visually, and are very instantaneously distinctive. I was really thrown a curve-ball, cause I did not expect the 2nd level to be in a science lab of some sorts, not whatsoever. It's a really crazy twist -- yet it just works so well. It's a huge contrast to the former level, but it still works alongside it.

Deadlink's soundtrack is just straight-up... "wow." I'm shocked, I'm surprised.
The soundtrack for Deadlink truly blew me away with its score, and I'm simply amazed.
Ivory Tower Soundworks did such brilliant works on it all, and there's not a single bad song. All of them are true bonerjams & extraordinary headbangers! They're on-par with something like Cyberpunk 2077's in-game combat music as well -- which is insane!
[url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gAdJvGW9rPE&ab_channel=GrubyEntertainment ]My favourite one so far is definitely 'Hòmo Patent'<3 [/url]
Great stuff, man. I'd utmost recommend everyone to check the soundtrack out!
I'm so glad Gruby Entertainment themselves upload their own tracks, instead of us having to rely on compressed sound-files extracted from the game files, lol.



[h1] Conclusion [/h1]

Deadlink blew me away. I played the short-time demo & thought it was 'alright'. Then I bought it upon release... didn't really care... meh. 30 minutes later & I'm standing up, sweating, headbanging, and grinning from the sheer amount of pure joy I'm experiencing!

[b] HUGE [/b] recommendations for all those interested! Even as a rogue-lite hater, this stands as a likely GOTY candidate for me.
I can't wait to see what's next for this game!

Fun game, cool mechanics; probably didn't need to be a roguelike imo, and could definitely use some loadout customization.

Beyond gameplay though, the aesthetics are amazing; I dev in UE5, the use of post processing in this game is legitimately amazing; the AI is impressive, movement feels great, the effects are very impressive. None of this is stuff built into UE5, if you're not a AAA studio you've gotta fight the engine to get things looking this good. None of the marketplace assets are made for this art style, you can tell everything here was made by hand.

Overall, the game is very polished when it comes to gun play. Certain abilities are fun enough. But There's multiple things it lacks in. When you play a FPS roguelite, you're usually wanting to test out different weapons, but each character only has two. What if you don't like either of them? You have to play enough with two guns you don't like to unlock the next character. Which relates to my next point. In this game it is essential to use your abilities to progress in the game. What if those abilities aren't to your play style? Too bad. I understand this game is trying to do something different which I can appreciate but personally it feels too constrictive. Go play RoboQuest or Hellfire Reborn.

Every class of "shell" has its own play style related to their abilities and load out, after you figure out what that style [b]IS[/b] the game finally becomes fun.

Good luck grinding those hub upgrades, the game can be ridiculous without them, they're quite expensive too.

I know I'll keep coming back to this on and off, if you get Deadlink get it half off and try not to pull your hair out on those first couple of runs.

I really wish there was a middling option for reviews, I'm very conflicted about this game, I'll just spit out a pros and cons list and you can make of it what you will.

PROS:

-Gamefeel is incredible. The movement, the way the guns shoot, the sounds, the animations, it all comes together in a way that's just immaculate. This game scratches a movement shooter itch that only ultrakill has previously scratched for me.

-Related to gamefeel, class mechanics are fun and feel really good. A lot of these mechanics are versatile and have many use cases, allowing the player to have a lot of freedom in their gameplay. For example the hunter shell's switchback, which lets you switch places with an enemy, stunning them in the process. Pretty simple and yet very versatile. 

-The combat music is great, banger high energy synths that roll with the fighting.

CONS:

-While the enemy design is usually great, the boss design can feel crusty at times, certain class abilities just don't work on them, meaning shells which rely more on these abilities have a harder time. The game also can fall in the pit of "more health = harder", leading to boss encounters that can feel like a slog to get through, and something that has to be endured to get to the fun part that's after them rather than part of the fun themselves. Trinary Iskra for example, while a very interesting concept (3 AI cores in one machine which are constantly bickering with each other) basically just boils down to a parkour challenge, it spins lasers around in patterns and makes platforms you have to jump between while you whittle away at its health bar. Its not particularly difficult but it takes a while and isn't very engaging the way the rest of the game is.

-Repetition, it all kinda gets old after a while. The gameplay feels good enough to stay fresh, but the rooms and enemies start to feel stale. There is one preset boss per region, it never changes. You can fight optional bosses as challenges, but they are just re-skins of already existing enemies.

-Finally, the writing. It's not good. Now its a rogue-lite, the focus and appeal is on the gameplay, the story is secondary, this is a given. Unfortunately, the lore often drifts from being poorly written into straight up being gross, to the point it makes it harder to enjoy the rest of the game. I will explain, now as is par for the course with poorly written cyberpunk there is an unhealthy dose of techno-orientalism, and at a glance one might think that's as bad as it gets. It is not. i.e. the codex entry of one of the basic yakuza enemies in the japan region describes them as "trying to outdo each other in their show of suicidal dedication". Subtle. There is also the megacorps, the story is about taking down megacorps. Sick right? Unfortunately it turns out the megacorps are written less like actual corporations and more like what your politically illiterate conservative grandfather would criticize as "the elite", in that they for example, employ women. No I'm not kidding. The final region has two kinds of basic enemies, one is all guys and one is all girls. The women 'caste' or whatever are described in the codex as a "propaganda force." Because they're women. The company hires 50% women. And it's framed by the writing as like, dystopian. Do you get what I mean now?

TL:DR
Feels incredible to play most of the time, very engaging gameplay that rewards quick thinking and creativity, music slaps, however the bosses can be a slog, surroundings feel stale after a few hours, and you have to actively tune out the really gross writing.
